Fugueuses – un cri d'alarme lancé depuis: Runaways – A Cry for Help from the Centre jeunesse de Laval
Au moins trois des quatres jeunes filles: At least three of the four girls reported missing in early February in the Montréal region are placed at the Centre jeunesse de Laval.
Salut, c’est Lela avec Loubna et Christe: Hi, it’s Lela, with Loubna and Christelle!
Au début du mois, une image montrant les: Earlier this month, an image showing the faces of several missing teenagers circulated widely across Quebec. From that moment, we understood that it was essential to look into this issue. What is happening in Montréal? Why are so many teenagers disappearing in such a short time?
J’ai rapidement contacté Christelle pour: I quickly contacted Christelle to propose that she work on the story with us. In the first few days, I made several calls to frontline workers we know in order to better understand the situation. One of them pointed me to Shayna’s video, which had been posted the day before. After watching it, I reached out to the young woman to propose an interview. She accepted. Less than 24 hours after the video went online, Christelle and I were at Shayna’s home in Laval. For more than an hour, she opened up to us with great vulnerability. Her mother then told us about her own experience at the Centre jeunesse de Laval.
Depuis la prise de parole de Shayna, d’a: Since Shayna spoke out, other girls placed in youth centres have decided to share their own stories. Her video, picked up by several social media accounts, prompted reactions and numerous comments from young people who have lived in youth centres. Loubna gathered several of these testimonies. One by one, the two women she met told her about their time in a youth centre, sometimes for the first time.
Elle a également tenté d’obtenir une ent: She also tried to obtain an interview with the management of the CISSS de Laval, which oversees the Centre jeunesse de Laval. That proved impossible: after several exchanges over several days, by email and by phone, she was ultimately turned down. We regret not having been able to conduct this interview, which would have shed a different light on the subject.
Ce reportage a en quelque sorte ouvert u: This report opened a Pandora’s box, in a way. It was hard to set limits, so numerous and so heavy were the stories. We decided to continue our work by preparing a second report.
En tant que journalistes, nous avons res: As journalists, we felt the weight of these testimonies and the need to document these stories. We thank everyone who shared their experiences with us. This is only the beginning of the conversation.
« On ne fugue pas de chez nous, on fugue: “We don’t run away from home, we run away from the centre” – An investigation into a system in crisis
Au début du mois, les visages de sept ad: Earlier this month, the faces of seven missing teenagers circulated widely on social media and in the media across Quebec. Their similar ages, heights and weights quickly sparked speculation online, with some internet users raising the possibility of a human trafficking ring. A week later, all of the young people had been found.
En enquêtant sur ces disparitions, La Co: In investigating these disappearances, La Converse was able to confirm that at least three of the four girls are placed at the Centre jeunesse de Laval, in the girls’ unit, Notre-Dame de Laval (NDL). It is also known that at least one of the boys is in a youth centre. Since the start of the 2024-2025 period, which is still under way, the CISSS de Laval has already recorded 298 runaway incidents, compared with 231 for all of 2023-2024. But why do the girls run away from this facility so often? What do they go through inside these walls? Investigation.
Le soleil tape fort sur le stationnement: The sun beats down on the parking lot of the Centre jeunesse de Laval. Around it, cars come and go. Across the street are a few businesses and a neighbourhood police station, strategically placed. The building is massive, cold, intimidating. Standing in front of it, it is hard to ignore the impression it gives: a prison.
Le centre se compose de 12 unités, sépar: The centre is made up of 12 units, separating boys and girls. On the left, a small yellow building catches the eye. Regulars call it NDL, for Notre-Dame de Laval. It has room for 110 girls aged 12 to 17. The buildings’ balconies are fenced in, turned into cages hanging over several floors. Teenage girls can sometimes be seen there, staring into the distance. Behind the centre, a park leads to the école Mont-de-La Salle, where several of the centre’s girls go to school. This ordinary space becomes a high-risk passageway. In just a few metres, you pass from one world to another. On one side, quiet residential streets; on the other, a locked structure, a place where you enter and that some try to escape.
« Ils m’ont enfermée en isolement pendan: “They locked me in isolation for 12 hours”
Dans la nuit de jeudi à vendredi, le 7 f: In the night of Thursday to Friday, February 7, Shayna posted a video on social media. In front of the camera, she denounces what she is living through at the Centre jeunesse de Laval, and says she knows the girls who were reported missing until last week. She describes degrading treatment, including full strip searches and prolonged periods of forced isolation.
Elle évoque des comportements qu’elle co: She describes behaviour she considers unjustified and explains that the girls who ran away did not flee their homes, but the youth centre they were in together. “All these girls disappeared because of the centre (…) I want to say that, because of the centre, the girls who disappeared are putting themselves in danger, they’re getting into prostitution stuff… Because they don’t know where to go anymore, and that’s exactly what the pimps are looking for right now; so they make them sell their bodies,” says the teenager. When she woke up Friday morning, her video had gone viral.
Le soir même, on rencontre Shayna chez e: That same evening, we met Shayna at her home with her mother, where she spends her weekends. At the family home in Laval, we found a calm, thoughtful and articulate teenager. She carries herself like a ballet dancer and, looking at her, you can tell she has a flair for fashion. For more than an hour, Shayna told us about her life at the Centre jeunesse de Laval. She has been placed there on and off since she was nine years old. Now 16, she has lived at NDL for seven years. She has run away nine times.
« Il faut attendre une sortie. Moi, je s: “You have to wait for an outing. Me, I go out from Friday night to Sunday night,” she says. “On Sunday night, instead of going back to the centre, I would leave. The goal was to show that I wasn’t running away from home, but from the centre. That’s why I never left before Sunday night. Every time I left, or was declared a runaway, it was on a Sunday night,” she explains. She insists on this point. And she is not alone. Of the four girls who went missing at the beginning of the year, two also ran away on a Sunday, one on a Saturday and another on a Monday.
En octobre dernier, après une sortie à l: Last October, after an outing to the beach, Shayna says she was placed in isolation for 12 hours for refusing a <l1>full strip search</l1>. “Cold air was coming through the window, which was screwed shut, and an air conditioner was blowing nonstop. It felt like I was outside,” she describes. Dressed in a bathing suit, she shivered, unable to drink, eat or use the toilet. “I have <l2>sickle cell anemia</l2>, it’s very dangerous,” she adds. At the end of her strength, she says she finally gave in to the search so as not to miss a visit from her father. “They didn’t find anything on me.” Traumatized by the experience, she filed a complaint against the institution and is waiting to learn when she will appear in court.
Un dimanche, Shayna fugue avec deux fill: One Sunday, Shayna runs away with two girls from NDL, but police intercept her before she is even declared a runaway. When she returns, she is placed in a reflection room. When she gets upset, the officers escort her to “la marée” (“the tide”), a calming room where she is supposed to spend 30 minutes. After the half hour, she is told she has to stay longer because of “the group’s agitation.” Her stay is extended. “I ended up falling asleep and stayed there for 3 hours instead of the planned 30 minutes.” For two days, she asks for explanations, but is told it was a communication error. “I didn’t file a complaint because it was only three hours… but I guarantee you I’ve been through more than that.”
Trois semaines plus tard, elle fugue de: Three weeks later, she runs away again with four girls, one of them from NDL. On the third day, feeling in danger, she sends her address to her mother, who finds her. “They were about to send her to Toronto,” her mother tells us. When she returns to the centre, Shayna has to go through a “bedbug protocol,” which requires her to remove her clothes to prevent any infestation. Refusing to undress in front of someone, she is placed in isolation for nine hours in one of the centre’s three isolation rooms. “I arrived at 3 a.m. and got out at 12:30 p.m.” She reports that she was woken every 15 minutes and asked whether she had changed her mind. A youth worker who had supported her in the past finally steps in. “She came back at 12:30 and said: ‘Get up, this makes no sense anymore. Go change in the bathroom and go to sleep.’ I still had to do nine hours of isolation, and it bothers me.”
Unité Notre-Dame de Laval au Centre jeun: Notre-Dame de Laval unit at the Centre jeunesse de Laval. Photo: Amélie Rock
Shayna prend la parole pour dénoncer des: Shayna is speaking out to denounce practices she finds unacceptable. “I made mistakes that brought me to a youth centre, but that doesn’t mean I deserve to be treated like this,” she says indignantly. She believes the treatment of young people pushes some of them to run away. According to her, there is always a girl on the run, and it never happens that everyone is there at the same time.
Selon ce qu’elle a pu observer, les fugu: From what she has observed, the girls who run away are often long-term residents. “They try to leave the centre, but no one helps them. Before looking for the girls who run away, the centre should give them a reason to want to come back.”
Mais les risques sont immenses. « Être e: But the risks are immense. “Being on the run means living with fear: where to sleep, when to eat, how to survive? There are always bad trips, moments of panic. And running from the police is a constant weight.” All the more so because another threat lurks: pimping networks. “All vulnerable teenagers are exposed to it, but for a girl from a centre, it’s even easier to get sweet-talked. You think they want what’s best for you.”
La façon dont les éducateurs s’adressent: The way youth workers speak to the young people feeds the unease, Shayna believes. “At the centre, you don’t have the right to your opinion. They control everything, even when you want to go to the bathroom.” Conversations between the young people are also monitored, and they can be punished for an “unclear contact.” “It’s an abuse of power. I need to talk, to confide in someone.”
Elle dénonce aussi l’usage de la force p: She also denounces the use of force by security officers. “I saw a girl carried by four officers, her head pressed against the wall. Her nose and her ear were bleeding.” Shayna questions these practices: “A friend was crying. They took her up to isolation and told her she wouldn’t get out as long as she was crying. But they didn’t give her any breathing technique, nothing. How does that help anyone?”
Shayna raconte comment ces traitements l: Shayna describes how this treatment affected her. “I started having fits of anger. I had a rage I couldn’t control.” Today, she says she is doing better, but the road was hard. “Learning to manage your anger in a place where everything is controlled, and then going back into a freer world, it’s a shock,” she explains.
Stefania, la mère de Shayna, s’installe: Stefania, Shayna’s mother, sits down next to her daughter. Their two stories echo each other. She is only 37. Like her daughter, she knew life in a youth centre during her adolescence. Of her five children, four have been placed at the Centre jeunesse de Laval. Today, she feels that her past, marked by DPJ interventions, has followed her into her parenting.
« Je me suis fait abuser sexuellement à: “I was sexually abused at 14. I asked for help at school, and that’s when the DPJ came into my life,” she says. Because of the trauma caused by the abuse, Stefania was no longer herself. “They said I had violent behaviour. But they didn’t know what I had been through.”
Stefania a alors été retirée de sa famil: Stefania was then removed from her family by the DPJ and placed. “I thought it was a good thing – then I went through the system: foster family, group home, open centre, secure centre…” she explains. “My mother fought hard, and then she didn’t have the strength to fight anymore.”
Elle aussi est placée à NDL, et dit avoi: She too was placed at NDL, and says she experienced abuse at the centre. “It’s been years since I went through these things, and only now am I able to open up. To do searches, they put me on the floor, they put their foot in my face, it was really very violent…”
À 16 ans, Stefania fugue avec une fille: At 16, Stefania ran away with a girl from NDL. Over the next two years, she joined a network controlled by a pimp and began working for the procurer. “It was the same recruitment system; I met a girl who said we could find ways to run away together,” she says, fearing that her daughter will be recruited in the same way.
Il arrivait à Stefania de rentrer d’elle: Stefania sometimes returned to the youth centre on her own, especially if she felt in danger. She would then make sure the police were not alerted: “If it’s the police who find you and bring you back to the youth centre, the consequences are more serious. You can spend three months without leaving the centre, with only visiting rights.”
« Je veux faire tomber le centre jeuness: “I want to bring down the youth centre. I want it destroyed and rebuilt. With good people, who have good values.” - Stephania
Dans le centre jeunesse, se projeter ver: In a youth centre, imagining a future is a challenge. For some girls, prostitution and crime seem to be the only way out. Stefania believes the repression experienced in these institutions pushes many young people to develop behavioural problems, reinforcing a cycle that is hard to break. According to her, young people are all the more inclined to run away because they see the image of the runaway glorified by popular culture, with shows like Fugueuse and La décadence de Montréal. “People want to be like that. Now they want to become like the singer Enima,” she laments.
Il est près de 20 h, et le téléphone de: It is nearly 8 p.m., and Stefania’s phone rings, interrupting the conversation. A caseworker from the youth centre says that Shayna has to be back by 10 p.m., with no advance notice. The teenager thought she could spend the weekend here at her mother’s, as usual. On the couch, her hands are shaking. She is afraid of paying for her viral video when she goes back to NDL. Her mother manages to negotiate with the caseworker. In the end, Shayna will spend the weekend at her mother’s.
Stefania souhaite se servir de son expér: Stefania wants to use her experience to speak to the mothers of young people who are in youth centres. “We all made mistakes, telling ourselves they’ll learn from the centre. You’re on the wrong track,” she says vehemently. “The centre is not the option; working together, that’s the option! With the specialists, the DPJ – yes, there are good caseworkers, they’re not all bad – but if you go against each other, nothing will come of it.”
Aujourd’hui, elle travaille en relation: Today, she works in the helping professions and is pursuing studies in that field. “I’m the person who can best understand people. That’s why I chose this path.” Despite her commitment, she refuses to work in a youth centre. The pain is still too raw. “If I saw children being mistreated there, I don’t know what I would be capable of doing.”
Elle ne mâche pas ses mots envers l’inst: She does not mince words about the institution where she spent her adolescence, and where her children lived in spite of her. “I want to bring down the youth centre. I want it destroyed and rebuilt. With good people, who have good values,” she says.
La mère de famille souhaite que les jeun: The mother wants young people to be able to communicate freely with their peers and help one another. But in her view, it starts with their guardians. “If we, as adults, don’t support each other, the young people won’t see that as an example,” she points out. “What needs to be done, in my opinion, is to talk with young people a lot. Locking them up is not the solution.”
Stephania se mobilise pour Shayna après: Stephania has rallied around Shayna since she spoke out. “The centre called me to say that they could go after her, that it could be damage to their reputation,” she laments. She is not letting it get her down, though. “They’re trying to put pressure on us, and I’m not going to give in, not this time.”
La vidéo de Shayna semble avoir donné du: Shayna’s video seems to have given courage to other young people, who are now sharing their own stories. Messages of support and testimonies have poured in. “There are 40-year-olds who told me it hasn’t changed. It’s not normal for you to tell me you went through the same thing as me. Where’s the progress?” asks Shayna. Many young women who have been through different youth centres denounce an environment marked by violence, isolation and a glaring lack of resources. Some speak out using the hashtag #SurvivantedeCentreJeunesse. We gathered the testimonies of two former residents of the Centre jeunesse de Laval.
« C’est la première fois que je raconte: “This is the first time I’m telling what I went through. I arrived there on the 25th of the month… There are dates like that you never forget,” Alex* says quietly. Now 27, they spent just over a year at the Centre jeunesse de Laval, from 2011 to 2012. They are speaking out today so that things change: “For me, it was over 10 years ago and nothing has changed. The public needs to know the reality of what goes on in those places, because people have no idea, and there is a lot of judgment and prejudice toward the young people who are there.”
Selon Alex, il est important de comprend: According to Alex, it is important to understand that these young people do not run away from home, but from a centre that allegedly fails to fulfill its mission of psychosocial support and where there are sometimes cases of mistreatment. “I ran away several times, and you have to understand that these young people who ran away think nobody loves them, that nobody is on their side in these centres, while on the outside, certain networks take advantage of their fragility to lure them into illegal activities.”
C’est à l’âge de 13 ans qu' Alex découvr: Alex was 13 when they first came to the Centre jeunesse de Laval. They had “behavioural problems” that their mother “couldn’t manage,” and their father was absent. Placed first at the Centre de réadaptation pour jeunes en difficulté d’adaptation Dominique-Savio, which has a more flexible approach, they were taken to the Centre jeunesse de Laval one autumn evening. “Obviously, they decided I needed a stricter framework,” they explain.
À son arrivée, Alex se plie à une fouill: On arrival, Alex submits to a standard search and is taken to their new living space. For the 13-year-old, it is a shock. “The room looked a lot more like a prison cell than anything else. The bed was a shelf fixed to the wall with a really thin mattress on it. There was a shelf fixed to the wall as a desk, and the only other piece of furniture was a chair.” Alex says that during their stay, their room was “completely turned upside down” twice as part of drug searches.
Plus douloureux pour Alex, iel se souvie: Even more painful for Alex is the memory of the day they learned of their grandfather’s death. “I was 13, and the support to grieve wasn’t there. They told me: ‘It’s not important, he was just your grandfather.’ They let me out for one day for the funeral and that’s it, I had to deal with it all on my own,” Alex laments.
Iel a surtout été marquée par la solitud: Above all, they were marked by the loneliness and the damaging effects of a constant lack of social relationships. “We were never allowed to talk without someone supervising. So I quickly made myself small, because I was terrified of being sent somewhere even worse. I followed every rule, I never tried to sneak in anything forbidden, I did everything I could to leave as fast as possible. And even then, I still spent more than a whole year in deep distress,” they say.
Celle qui est aujourd’hui vendeus.e en l: Now working as a bookstore clerk, Alex found refuge in the books of the Centre jeunesse de Laval’s small library: “We were allowed two or three books a week, and I always picked the biggest ones I could find, no matter the subject, just to escape a little. From my room, I could hear the girls screaming. Sometimes some of them would disappear, and we wouldn’t see them again for two months.”
Alex dénonce le placement d’enfants dont: Alex condemns the placement of children whose problems or life stories were not suited to these particularly restrictive closed units. “Looking back, it’s clear it wasn’t a place for me, and it didn’t help me at all. I was 13, the youngest in the group, the others were 15 to 17 and were there for drug or prostitution issues, while I just had trouble managing my emotions, but I never hurt anyone or was violent,” they say.
Près de 15 ans après son séjour au Centr: Nearly 15 years after their stay at the Centre jeunesse de Laval, Alex says they cannot think back on that period of their life without struggling with complex post-traumatic stress disorder linked to their experiences, but also, in part, to their time at the Centre jeunesse de Laval. “I’m doing better today, but I don’t understand how we’re still at this point, with young girls continuing to go through this. This is not how you protect children.”
Gabriela a passé une semaine à NDL en 20: Gabriela spent a week at NDL in 2024. She has painful memories of those few days. “How do I describe it? It’s a prison for kids. Never, truly never, have I felt so alone! I just wanted to get out of there,” confides the 17-year-old, who now lives in a supervised apartment.
Élevée depuis son jeune âge par ses gran: Raised from a young age by her grandparents, in a house where her uncle and aunt also lived, Gabriela was not lucky enough to be born into a family cocoon conducive to her development. She says she suffered a first sexual assault at 12, when a relative kissed her by force “with tongue” during a vacation in the South. “And then, I went through physical violence and insults at home from some members of my family,” she says without faltering.
Elle réunit alors tout son courage pour: She then gathered all her courage to confide in her school’s social worker about what she was going through, who filed a report with the DPJ. “I was 13 at that point. The school told me it was going to call my grandparents to inform them of the report, and I warned them that, either way, I wasn’t going home.” She ran away to a friend’s place. “I went to a friend’s house, with her parents, and two weeks later, they came knocking at the door,” she remembers. “They” were the police officers sent by the DPJ. When she got into their vehicle, she didn’t yet know it, but she was headed to the Centre jeunesse de Laval.
« Quand je suis arrivée au centre jeunes: “When I got to the youth centre, I didn’t even know what it was, but I knew it was a place where I didn’t want to be,” Gabriela says quietly. She says that after being taken to a small room, she was told to undress and put on a hospital gown. “They held a towel in front of me, and I took everything off. They put my things in a garbage bag and told me to do jumping jacks, to check that I wasn’t hiding anything anywhere.” She then put on the clothes she was given and was taken to her room.
«Ces centres ne sont pas adaptés ! Quand: “These centres aren’t suited to young people! When some kids need help, they don’t get it. I was there even though I hadn’t done anything, and on top of that nobody tried to help me or find out if I was okay.” – Gabriela
« C’est une toute petite pièce sans aucu: “It’s a tiny room with no windows at all! On the door, there are several holes with no glass and a curtain, so they can watch and listen at any time,” she describes. “At that point they gave me reflection exercises: they’re questions on a sheet of paper that you have to answer, otherwise you can’t get out. I had to say why I was there, what I needed to improve… when I was a victim!”
Elle assure que les jeunes filles doiven: She says the girls must ask permission for every action, including going to the bathroom, and that sometimes they have to wait a long time before being allowed to go. “The whole week, I was never able to shower with hot water, there was only cold water. I couldn’t talk to anyone, and since they hadn’t planned to put me in either the in-house school or the outside school, I was left alone in my room all day with crossword puzzles,” she describes.
Elle estime qu’après avoir dénoncé des f: She believes that after reporting serious acts within her family, she did not get the support she needed. “I think every young person, despite their problems, needs to talk. But if a young person doesn’t feel comfortable talking with the centre’s social workers, it’s because there’s a problem,” says the young woman. “These centres aren’t suited to young people! When some kids need help, they don’t get it. I was there even though I hadn’t done anything, and on top of that nobody tried to help me or find out if I was okay.”
Parler pour toutes les autres: Speaking out for all the others
Du haut de ses 16 ans, et forte de son e: At 16, and strengthened by her experience, Shayna is determined: “I’d wanted to do this for a while, but I was too young,” she says calmly. “I’m going to talk about it as much as I can.”
L’adolescente revient sur son cas.« Plus: The teenager returns to her case. “Several times, I asked to file a complaint. I was told the complaints were in progress,” she laments, as nothing seems to move forward. According to her, the responsible adults doubt her account. She condemns the legal system, which, in her view, offers no support. She wants to leave the youth centre and says her lawyer is struggling to follow up. “I started my steps in October, I’ve been waiting a long time.” She does not feel heard during the proceedings. “In front of the judge, we only talked about everything I’d done wrong, but never about the reasons behind my report. When I talked about the abuse, they said this wasn’t the time to talk about that and that it would be in another court. Every time, it was pushed back to later.”
Shayna souhaite s’adresser directement a: Shayna wants to speak directly to the institutions. “I would tell them to re-evaluate their code of conduct. The centres’ rules date from a really long time ago. Yes, it has to be strict, but there are limits! Some rules that don’t really make sense need to change,” she says.
Plus tard, l’adolescente souhaite travai: Later on, the teenager wants to work in fashion design. “And keep speaking up for the people in youth centres. I’d like to change some things in youth centres. Even though I have my passion on the side: design.”
Contactée par La Converse, la direction: When contacted by La Converse, the management of the CISSS that runs the Centre jeunesse de Laval first refused to grant us an interview. After agreeing in principle to an interview, the communications department ultimately informed La Converse that the Director of Youth Protection, Jean-François Payette, was “not available” because he was travelling abroad.
Nous avons alors sollicité une entrevue: We then requested an interview with the youth program director, Anick Deslongchamps, who was also “not available” because of the 48-hour notice we had proposed. La Converse then offered to postpone the interview, but no representative seemed any more available, not the following week, nor the one after that, nor the one after that…
Nous avons donc envoyé 15 questions au C: We therefore sent 15 questions to the CISSS de Laval. The only response we received was the following statement: “The CISSS de Laval is committed to providing a safe environment for all users in its care. With this in mind, since December 16, an external support person, Manon Saint-Maurice, appointed by the National Director of Youth Protection, has been assisting the CISSS de Laval to help teams analyze and reduce the use of control measures. This joint decision between the CISSS de Laval and the National Director stems from a desire to act on issues concerning the use of control measures and thus ensure the well-being of children and respect for their rights.”
Nous n’avons obtenu aucune réponse aux q: We received no answers to the questions about the abuse reported by the girls and women we met for this report.
Questionné au sujet des fugues de l’unit: Asked about runaways from the Notre-Dame de Laval unit of the youth centre and the emergency measures taken to supervise young people, the office of the Minister of Social Services, Lionel Carmant, said that “many runaway episodes are very short and do not pose a danger to the teenagers involved.” It adds that these runaways can “originate from several different motives, for example a need for freedom, for validation, for experimentation, for escape, for protest, for a search for identity or autonomy. However, some teenagers may be in danger, notably girls, who may sometimes be at risk of sexual exploitation.”
Dans la deuxième partie de ce dossier, n: In the second part of this series, we will explore the systemic dimension of the failures of youth centres.
